nodes.label: Yellow onion
nodes.note: Long-day varieties (Copra, Patterson) are the right type for northern Ohio.

nodes.label: Shallot
nodes.sow: Plant sets in October or April

nodes.label: Garlic
nodes.sow: Plant cloves mid-October, mulch with straw
nodes.harvest: Mid-July when the lower third of leaves brown
nodes.note: The single highest-value thing to grow in Ohio: plant once in fall, ignore it all winter, harvest a year of garlic.

nodes.label: Carrots
nodes.sow: Direct sow late April and again in July
nodes.harvest: 70 days; fall carrots after frost are sweeter

nodes.label: Red bell pepper
nodes.sow: Start indoors March 1, transplant after May 20
nodes.harvest: August–September; leave green peppers on the plant to turn red

nodes.label: Broccoli
nodes.harvest: Spring and fall; side shoots keep coming after the main head

nodes.label: Cauliflower
nodes.sow: Transplant August 1 for a fall crop

nodes.label: Zucchini
nodes.note: Two plants feed a family of four and half the neighborhood. Pick at 6-8 inches.

nodes.label: Butternut squash
nodes.harvest: October; cures and stores until February in a cool room

nodes.label: Roma tomatoes
nodes.note: Paste types (San Marzano, Amish Paste) are the ones worth the space — they cook down into sauce.

nodes.label: Cherry tomatoes
nodes.note: Sungold is the variety that turns kids into tomato eaters. One plant in a large pot is enough.

nodes.label: Baby spinach
nodes.sow: Direct sow late March and again September 1
nodes.harvest: Spring and fall; bolts in July heat

nodes.label: Lacinato kale
nodes.harvest: June through December — survives Ohio snow and gets sweeter after frost

nodes.label: Swiss chard
nodes.harvest: June–November, cut outer leaves and it regrows all season

nodes.label: Arugula
nodes.harvest: 25 days — the fastest thing in the garden

nodes.label: Cremini mushrooms
nodes.tips: Do not crowd the pan and do not salt them until they brown — that is the whole secret.

nodes.label: Green beans
nodes.sow: Direct sow after May 20, again in early July
nodes.harvest: 55 days; pick every other day or they get tough

nodes.label: Asparagus
nodes.sow: Plant crowns April, first real harvest in year three
nodes.note: A permanent bed that produces for 20 years. Plant it once.

nodes.label: Brussels sprouts
nodes.harvest: After the first hard frost in November

nodes.label: Sugar snap peas
nodes.sow: Direct sow April 1 (St. Patrick's Day planting works here)

nodes.label: Fennel bulb
nodes.sow: Direct sow July 1 for a fall bulb crop

nodes.label: Beets
nodes.sow: Direct sow April and again August
nodes.harvest: 55 days; the greens are as good as chard

nodes.label: Lemon
nodes.tips: Acid is the single best substitute for salt. When a dish tastes flat, it usually needs lemon, not more salt.

nodes.label: Apples
nodes.note: Northeast Ohio is orchard country — Patterson Fruit Farm and Szalay's are closer than a spray schedule is worth.

nodes.label: Blueberries
nodes.sow: Plant bushes in spring, acidify the soil
nodes.note: Ohio soil runs alkaline; blueberries need pH 4.5-5.5, so plant them in a dedicated bed with peat and pine bark.

nodes.label: Fresh ginger
nodes.tips: Freeze the knob whole and grate it frozen on a microplane — no peeling, no waste.

nodes.label: Cilantro
nodes.harvest: Bolts fast in heat — succession sowing is the only way

nodes.label: Flat-leaf parsley
nodes.tips: A handful of chopped parsley over anything is the cheapest way to make home food look plated.

nodes.label: Fresh basil
nodes.note: Pinch the flower tips weekly and one plant supplies pesto all summer. Grows happily in a pot by the back door.

nodes.label: Fresh mint
nodes.sow: Plant in a pot, never in the ground
nodes.note: Mint will colonize a garden bed in two seasons. Container only.

nodes.label: Fresh dill
nodes.sow: Direct sow April, self-seeds forever after

nodes.label: Fresh rosemary
nodes.harvest: Year-round if you bring the pot indoors — it will not survive an Ohio winter outside

nodes.label: Fresh thyme
nodes.harvest: Perennial here — survives zone 6 winters and comes back every year

nodes.label: Eggs (large)
nodes.heartNote: Current AHA guidance treats one egg a day as fine for most healthy adults; for someone managing existing heart disease, keeping whole eggs to about 4 a week and using extra whites is the common recommendation.

nodes.label: Plain nonfat Greek yogurt
nodes.tips: Replaces sour cream and mayo one-for-one and adds 10 g of protein per half cup.

nodes.label: Unsweetened soy milk
nodes.heartNote: Soy is the only common plant milk with protein comparable to dairy, and FDA allows a qualified heart-health claim for soy protein.

nodes.label: Parmesan cheese
nodes.heartNote: Very high sodium and saturated fat, but you only need a tablespoon or two — used as a finisher, not a filler.
nodes.dietNote: True Parmigiano-Reggiano uses animal rennet. For a strict vegetarian, buy a domestic parmesan labeled vegetarian, or use nutritional yeast.

nodes.label: Feta cheese
nodes.tips: Buy the block in brine, not pre-crumbled — better texture, and it lasts a month.

nodes.label: Sharp cheddar
nodes.heartNote: Sharp cheddar delivers more flavor per gram than mild, so you can use a third less for the same effect.

nodes.label: Unsalted butter
nodes.heartNote: 51% saturated fat. Used here only in teaspoon amounts as a finishing fat, where you can actually taste it.

nodes.label: Extra-firm tofu
nodes.tips: Press it 15 minutes under a cutting board and a heavy pot, then freeze and thaw it once for a chewier, meatier texture.

nodes.label: Tempeh
nodes.tips: Steam it 10 minutes before marinating — it removes the bitterness people blame tempeh for.

nodes.label: Chickpeas, canned no-salt-added
nodes.tips: Drained weight of a 15 oz can is about 250 g. Save the aquafaba.

nodes.label: Cannellini beans, canned no-salt-added
nodes.tips: Blend half a can into any soup and it turns creamy with no cream at all.

nodes.label: Brown lentils (dry)
nodes.tips: No soaking, 25 minutes, holds its shape. One dollar feeds four people.

nodes.label: Red lentils (dry)
nodes.tips: Collapses into a creamy purée in 15 minutes — this is what makes dal thick without any dairy.

nodes.label: Boneless skinless chicken thighs
nodes.tips: Thighs are cheaper, more forgiving, and only about 15 more calories per serving than breast.

nodes.label: Salmon fillet
nodes.heartNote: AHA recommends two servings of fatty fish per week for people managing heart disease. Salmon is the easiest way to hit that.

nodes.label: Shrimp (raw, peeled)
nodes.tips: Frozen raw shrimp thaw in 10 minutes under cool water and cook in 3 — the fastest omnivore add-on there is.

nodes.label: Top sirloin steak, lean
nodes.heartNote: Red meat is the one to keep occasional when heart disease is in the picture — think a 3-4 oz portion a couple times a month, sliced thin over a vegetable-forward plate rather than a slab on its own.

nodes.label: Italian chicken sausage
nodes.heartNote: One link carries roughly 600 mg sodium. Use one link split across four servings as a flavoring, not as the protein.

nodes.label: Quinoa (dry)
nodes.tips: Rinse it in a fine strainer or it tastes soapy. Toast it dry for 2 minutes before adding water.

nodes.label: Farro (dry)
nodes.tips: Cook it like pasta in plenty of salted water, 25 minutes, drain. Keeps 5 days and makes any bowl feel like a restaurant grain bowl.

nodes.label: Old-fashioned rolled oats
nodes.heartNote: The beta-glucan fiber in oats is one of the few foods with an FDA-authorized heart-health claim — about 3 g a day measurably lowers LDL.

nodes.label: Whole wheat pasta (dry)
nodes.tips: If the kids resist whole wheat, start with half whole wheat and half regular in the same pot.

nodes.label: Corn tortillas
nodes.tips: Char them straight on a gas burner for 20 seconds a side. That one step is the difference between a taco and a great taco.

nodes.label: Whole grain bread
nodes.heartNote: Bread is a top-3 sodium source in the American diet, not because it is salty-tasting but because we eat so much of it. Compare labels — good loaves run 110-150 mg a slice.

nodes.label: Panko breadcrumbs
nodes.tips: Toast panko in a dry skillet with a little olive oil and lemon zest, then scatter it over pasta or roasted vegetables. It is the crunch that makes a plate feel finished.

nodes.label: Cornstarch
nodes.tips: Tossing tofu or chicken in cornstarch before searing is the restaurant trick for a shatteringly crisp exterior without deep frying.

nodes.label: Crushed tomatoes, no salt added
nodes.tips: San Marzano-style whole peeled tomatoes crushed by hand beat every pre-crushed can. Two minutes of work.

nodes.label: Tomato paste
nodes.tips: Fry the paste in oil for 60 seconds until it darkens before adding liquid. That is where deep flavor comes from without meat. Buy the tube so it keeps.

nodes.label: Light coconut milk
nodes.heartNote: Coconut fat is highly saturated. Light coconut milk has about a third the saturated fat of full-fat and works fine in curries; stretch it with broth.

nodes.label: Low-sodium vegetable broth
nodes.heartNote: Regular broth runs 800-900 mg sodium per cup. Low-sodium runs 100-140. Switching is one of the biggest single sodium wins in home cooking.

nodes.label: Capers
nodes.tips: Rinse them. A rinsed tablespoon adds a huge pop of flavor for well under 100 mg of sodium.

nodes.label: Low-sodium marinara sauce
nodes.heartNote: Jarred sauces range from 90 to 650 mg sodium per half cup. Reading that one label changes a whole week of dinners.

nodes.label: Extra-virgin olive oil
nodes.heartNote: The PREDIMED trial found a Mediterranean diet with about 4 tablespoons of extra-virgin olive oil a day cut major cardiovascular events roughly 30% versus a low-fat diet. Olive oil is not the compromise here — it is the intervention.

nodes.label: Toasted sesame oil
nodes.tips: Finishing oil, not cooking oil. Add it off the heat or it turns bitter.

nodes.label: Dijon mustard
nodes.tips: A teaspoon of Dijon is what holds a vinaigrette together. It is also 55 mg of sodium — a rounding error next to bottled dressing.

nodes.label: Low-sodium soy sauce
nodes.heartNote: Even low-sodium soy sauce is about 530 mg per tablespoon. Use it as seasoning for a whole pan, not per plate, and skip the table bottle.

nodes.label: White miso paste
nodes.tips: Keeps a year in the fridge. A tablespoon whisked into a vinaigrette, a soup, or roasted vegetables adds the savory depth people think they need meat for.

nodes.label: Thai red curry paste
nodes.dietNote: Many brands contain shrimp paste. Maesri and Thai Kitchen make vegetarian versions — check the label.

nodes.label: Tahini
nodes.tips: Tahini plus lemon plus water plus garlic is a sauce that goes on everything. It seizes up before it loosens — keep whisking in water.

nodes.label: Pure maple syrup
nodes.tips: Northeast Ohio is maple country — local syrup from a Geauga or Summit County sugarhouse is a genuine upgrade.

nodes.label: Nutritional yeast
nodes.tips: The vegetarian answer to parmesan: same savory hit, no saturated fat, no sodium.

nodes.label: Raw almonds
nodes.heartNote: Roughly an ounce of nuts a day is one of the most consistent findings in cardiovascular nutrition — associated with meaningfully lower coronary heart disease risk.

nodes.label: Walnuts
nodes.heartNote: The only common nut with a meaningful amount of plant omega-3 (ALA) — about 2.5 g per ounce.

nodes.label: Raw cashews
nodes.tips: Soaked and blended, cashews make a cream sauce with no dairy at all.

nodes.label: Ground flaxseed
nodes.tips: Must be ground to absorb the omega-3s, and keep it in the freezer — it goes rancid fast.

nodes.label: Kosher salt
nodes.heartNote: A teaspoon of Diamond Crystal kosher salt is about 1,100 mg sodium; table salt is nearly double that per teaspoon because the crystals pack tighter. Recipes here salt the cooking water and the dish lightly and finish with acid instead.

nodes.label: Smoked paprika
nodes.tips: Smoke without meat. This is the spice that makes vegetarian beans and lentils taste like they have bacon in them.

nodes.label: Dried oregano
nodes.harvest: Perennial in zone 6 — comes back stronger every year and dries beautifully

nodes.label: Garam masala
nodes.tips: Add it at the end, not the beginning — it is a finishing blend and its aroma cooks off.

nodes.label: Fennel seed
nodes.tips: Fennel seed plus smoked paprika plus red pepper flakes is what makes mushrooms or lentils taste like Italian sausage.

nodes.label: Fresh cranberries
nodes.tips: Buy two bags in November and freeze one. They keep a year and cook straight from frozen.

nodes.label: Fresh sage
nodes.tips: Fry whole leaves in olive oil for 20 seconds until they go translucent and crisp. Best garnish of the autumn.

nodes.label: Fresh sage
nodes.harvest: Perennial in zone 6 — it comes back every spring and wants no attention

nodes.label: Watermelon
nodes.harvest: August — needs heat and room to sprawl

nodes.label: Chipotles in adobo
nodes.tips: Freeze leftovers in tablespoon blobs on parchment. A whole can never gets used at once.

nodes.label: Grapefruit
nodes.heartNote: Grapefruit interferes with several common medications, including some statins. If anyone at the table takes one, check with a pharmacist before making it a habit.

nodes.label: Unsweetened applesauce
nodes.tips: Swapping applesauce for half the oil in a quick bread keeps it moist and cuts the fat without anyone noticing.

shop.label: cans (14 oz) young green jackfruit in brine

nodes.label: Chives
nodes.sow: Seed or divide a clump in April
nodes.note: A perennial that comes back a little bigger every year and is the first green thing out of the ground in an Ohio spring. Cut it hard; it likes it.

nodes.label: January
tasks: Order seeds. Read the catalog by the fire; this is the whole point of January.
harvest: Nothing outdoors except stored squash, garlic, potatoes and onions

nodes.label: February
tasks: Start onion and leek seeds indoors under lights (Feb 1-15).

nodes.label: March
tasks: Start peppers and eggplant indoors March 1-10.
Direct sow spinach, arugula and peas outdoors in the last week if the soil can be worked.
harvest: Overwintered kale, if you mulched it

nodes.label: April
tasks: Start tomatoes indoors April 1.
Transplant broccoli, cabbage and lettuce outdoors mid-month.
Direct sow carrots, beets, radishes, chard and more spinach.
Plant seed potatoes.

nodes.label: May
tasks: Wait for the frost date. Transplant tomatoes, peppers, eggplant and basil after May 20.
Direct sow beans, cucumbers, zucchini and squash after May 20.
Plant sweet potato slips at the end of the month.

nodes.label: June
tasks: Mulch everything. Stake tomatoes before they need it.
Succession sow beans and cilantro.

nodes.label: July
tasks: Harvest garlic when the lower third of the leaves brown; cure it in a dry shaded place for two weeks.
Sow fall carrots and beets.
Water deeply twice a week rather than lightly every day.

nodes.label: August
tasks: Transplant fall broccoli, cabbage and kale August 1.
Sow spinach and lettuce for fall at the end of the month.
Preserve: freeze roasted tomatoes and pesto in ice cube trays.

nodes.label: September
tasks: Let peppers turn red on the plant — they double in sweetness.
Plant garlic beds' soil amendments now.

nodes.label: October
tasks: Plant garlic mid-month and mulch it with straw.
Cure winter squash in a warm room for 10 days before storing cool.
Bring the rosemary pot indoors before the first hard frost.

nodes.label: November
tasks: Mulch the kale and it will feed you through December.
Clean and oil tools.

nodes.label: December
tasks: Nothing. Rest.
harvest: Kale under snow, if you mulched

nodes.label: Weeknight Lentil Bolognese
nodes.blurb: The sauce that converts people. Lentils, a soffritto cooked past the point most people stop, and tomato paste fried until it darkens — it tastes like it simmered all afternoon.

nodes.label: Sheet-Pan Crispy Tofu and Broccoli, Sesame-Ginger Glaze
nodes.blurb: Cornstarch-dusted tofu that actually gets crisp in a home oven, broccoli with charred edges, and a glaze that goes on at the end so it never burns.

nodes.label: Chickpea Shakshuka
nodes.blurb: Eggs poached in a smoky pepper-tomato sauce with chickpeas for staying power. Twenty-five minutes, one skillet, and it feels like a restaurant brunch at 6pm.

nodes.label: Smoky Black Bean and Sweet Potato Tacos
nodes.blurb: Caramelized sweet potato, smoky beans, crunchy slaw, charred corn tortillas. The kind of taco night where nobody notices there's no meat.

nodes.label: 25-Minute Red Lentil Dal
nodes.blurb: Red lentils collapse into something creamy with no cream at all. Finished with a sizzling spice oil poured over at the table.

nodes.label: Mushroom Farro "Risotto"
nodes.blurb: All the comfort of risotto with a chewy whole grain and none of the standing-and-stirring. Deeply savory from properly browned mushrooms.

nodes.label: Tuscan White Bean and Kale Soup
nodes.blurb: Half the beans blended into the broth makes it creamy without a drop of cream. This is the pot to make on the first cold Sunday in October.

nodes.label: Pasta e Ceci
nodes.blurb: Roman pantry cooking: chickpeas, pasta, rosemary and a lot of olive oil, cooked in one pot until the starch turns the broth silky. Thirty minutes, seven dollars.

nodes.label: Charred Cauliflower Steaks with Romesco
nodes.blurb: Thick-cut cauliflower roasted until the edges go mahogany, over a smoky almond-pepper sauce that takes four minutes in a blender. This is the one to cook for company.

nodes.label: Garden Stir-Fry with Crisp Tofu
nodes.blurb: Whatever the garden or the crisper drawer is giving you, cooked hot and fast in a sauce built from four pantry bottles. Fifteen minutes once the prep is done.

nodes.label: Skillet Eggplant Parmesan
nodes.blurb: Roasted, not fried. Crisp panko goes on top at the end so it stays crunchy. All the comfort of the casserole with a third of the fat and half the dishes.

nodes.label: Butternut and Chickpea Curry
nodes.blurb: Sweet squash, creamy chickpeas, and a coconut broth that tastes like it took an hour. It takes thirty-five minutes and one pot.

nodes.label: Greek Quinoa Bowls with Whipped Feta
nodes.blurb: Everything cold and crunchy over warm quinoa, with a whipped feta that takes two minutes and tastes like a restaurant meze plate.

nodes.label: Friday Night Garden Pizza
nodes.blurb: Store-bought whole wheat dough, a hot stone or steel, and whatever is ripe. Everyone builds their own half, which is the entire point.

nodes.label: Summer Corn and Zucchini over Creamy Polenta
nodes.blurb: August on a plate. Sweet corn and blistered zucchini over soft polenta, with goat cheese melting into it.

nodes.label: Quinoa and Black Bean Stuffed Peppers
nodes.blurb: Make-ahead, freezer-friendly, and one of the few dinners that is genuinely as good reheated. Every pepper is a complete meal.

nodes.label: Miso Noodle Bowl with Bok Choy
nodes.blurb: A ten-minute broth that tastes like it simmered with bones. Miso goes in off the heat, which is the rule that makes or breaks it.

nodes.label: Three-Bean Smoky Chili
nodes.blurb: A spoonful of cocoa and a lot of smoked paprika do what a pound of beef used to. Better on day two, and it feeds a crowd for under ten dollars.

nodes.label: Za'atar Sheet-Pan Chickpeas and Vegetables with Tahini
nodes.blurb: One pan, twenty-five minutes in the oven, and a lemon-tahini sauce that makes it feel composed rather than thrown together.

nodes.label: Creamy Tomato Rigatoni with White Beans
nodes.blurb: The creaminess comes from blended cannellini beans, not cream — which also means 14 grams of protein and 9 grams of fiber a serving. Twenty-five minutes.

nodes.label: Skillet Black Bean Enchiladas
nodes.blurb: All the flavor of rolled enchiladas with none of the rolling. One skillet, thirty minutes, and the kids can pile on their own toppings.

nodes.label: Cold Peanut Noodles with Snap Peas and Edamame
nodes.blurb: Twenty minutes, no oven, and a peanut sauce that keeps a week in the fridge. The dinner for the night nobody wants to turn on the stove.

nodes.label: Slow-Roasted Salmon with Lemon, Dill and Asparagus
nodes.blurb: Roasted at 275°F so it never dries out and never turns the kitchen fishy. This is the two-fish-a-week recipe, and it is genuinely easier than the fast version.

nodes.label: Garden Frittata
nodes.blurb: Breakfast for dinner, built on whatever the garden gave you. Extra whites keep it light without making it taste like a diet.

nodes.label: Lentil-Mushroom Shepherd's Pie
nodes.blurb: The Sunday dinner. A deeply savory lentil and mushroom base under a sweet potato and Yukon mash. Worth the hour, and it makes two dinners.

nodes.label: Crispy Gnocchi with Brown Butter, Sage and White Beans
nodes.blurb: Skip the boiling water. Shelf-stable gnocchi dropped straight into a hot pan turns into little crisp-shelled pillows, and brown butter with fried sage is the sauce that ruins you for other sauces.

nodes.label: Real French Onion Soup
nodes.blurb: Five pounds of onions cooked down for the better part of an hour into something jammy and almost sweet, under a raft of bread and melted Gruyère. There is no shortcut and there does not need to be — the stove does the work while you do something else.

nodes.label: Chile Crisp Noodles with Jammy Eggs
nodes.blurb: Fifteen minutes, one pot, and a bowl of noodles slick with chili crisp and soy that tastes like something you would order out. The jammy egg on top is not optional in the way that things labelled optional usually are.

nodes.label: Mushroom Bourguignon
nodes.blurb: The braise that makes people go quiet at the table. Mushrooms browned hard, red wine reduced properly, and dried porcini doing the job that beef normally does. It tastes like it took all day and takes about an hour.

nodes.label: Baked Feta Pasta with Blistered Tomatoes
nodes.blurb: A block of feta in a dish of cherry tomatoes and olive oil, roasted until the tomatoes burst and the cheese slumps, then stirred into a sauce. It went round the world for a reason, and it is genuinely good.

nodes.label: Crispy Rice Bowl with Kimchi and a Fried Egg
nodes.blurb: Cold leftover rice pressed into a hot pan and left there until the bottom forms a golden crust you have to break with a spoon. Kimchi, a runny egg, and that crust — it is the best thing you can do with yesterday's rice.

nodes.label: Mushroom Birria Tacos with Consommé
nodes.blurb: Tortillas dipped in a deep red chile broth, griddled until the edges go crisp, and served with a cup of that same broth for dunking. It is a whole event, and the broth is what people remember.

nodes.label: Skillet Paneer Tikka Masala
nodes.blurb: Cubes of paneer browned in butter and folded into a tomato sauce built on bloomed garam masala. Restaurant tikka masala usually runs on a cup of cream; this one uses three tablespoons and gets the rest of its body from blended onion.

nodes.label: Sticky Gochujang Tofu
nodes.blurb: Tofu cornstarched and fried until the outside shatters, then tossed in a glaze that reduces to a lacquer in the pan. Cold cucumber salad on the side because something has to cut through it.

nodes.label: Harissa Butter Chickpeas over Garlic Yogurt
nodes.blurb: Chickpeas crisped in harissa butter, spooned over a pool of cold garlicky yogurt so it streaks pink where the two meet. Twenty minutes, mostly pantry, and it looks like something you would pay for.

nodes.label: Cacio e Pepe with Sweet Peas
nodes.blurb: Four ingredients and a technique. Pecorino, black pepper toasted in a dry pan, and starchy pasta water whisked into a sauce that clings like cream without any cream in it. Peas make it dinner rather than a side.

nodes.label: Charred Cabbage Steaks with Miso Butter
nodes.blurb: A three-dollar head of cabbage roasted hard until the outer leaves blacken and the inside goes sweet and silky, then brushed with miso butter. It is the cheapest thing in this collection and one of the best.

nodes.label: Heart-Smart Overnight Oats
nodes.blurb: Five minutes on Sunday night, four breakfasts done. Oat beta-glucan plus chia plus walnuts is about as heart-forward as a bowl gets.

nodes.label: The Green One
nodes.blurb: Three minutes, one blender, and it is genuinely green rather than green-adjacent. Flax and soy milk for the heart, frozen banana for the texture.

nodes.label: Soft Scrambled Eggs with Wilted Greens
nodes.blurb: Low and slow, off the heat before you think, with greens wilted into the pan first. Ten minutes and it eats like a hotel breakfast.

nodes.label: Blueberry Baked Oatmeal
nodes.blurb: Bake it Sunday, cut it into squares, and breakfast is handled through Thursday. Reheats in ninety seconds and tastes like a muffin.

nodes.label: Everything Avocado Toast with Smashed White Beans
nodes.blurb: The beans are what make it hold you until lunch — 15 grams of protein instead of 4, and it takes an extra ninety seconds.

nodes.label: Vanilla Chia Pudding
nodes.blurb: Four ingredients, ten seconds of stirring, and 10 grams of fiber per cup. The kids treat it as dessert; that is fine.

nodes.label: Smashed Chickpea Salad Sandwiches
nodes.blurb: Tastes like the tuna salad you grew up on, built on chickpeas and Greek yogurt instead of mayo. Fifteen minutes and it packs for lunch all week.

nodes.label: Greek Chickpea Jar Salads
nodes.blurb: Four lunches built in ten minutes on Sunday. Dressing on the bottom, greens on top, and nothing is soggy on Thursday.

nodes.label: Thermos Tomato-Lentil Soup
nodes.blurb: Thirty minutes, blends smooth, and holds heat in a thermos until noon. The lunch that gets a kid through a February school day.

nodes.label: Black Bean and Spinach Quesadillas
nodes.blurb: Twelve minutes, four ingredients you already have, and a vegetable the kids will not fight about because they cannot see it.

nodes.label: Build-a-Bowl (the Formula)
nodes.blurb: Not a recipe so much as an equation: grain plus roasted vegetable plus protein plus sauce plus crunch plus acid. Learn it once and you never need a recipe for lunch again.

nodes.label: Whipped Lemon Hummus
nodes.blurb: Ice water and a long blend are what make hummus fluffy instead of pasty. Five minutes, and it beats anything in a tub.

nodes.label: House Lemon-Dijon Vinaigrette
nodes.blurb: One jar, ninety seconds, and you never buy bottled dressing again. A quarter of the sodium and none of the additives.

nodes.label: Everything Tahini Sauce
nodes.blurb: The sauce that makes roasted vegetables into dinner. Four ingredients, two minutes, keeps a week.

nodes.label: Any-Vegetable Roast (the Method)
nodes.blurb: One temperature, one technique, every vegetable. This is the skill that makes vegetables the best thing on the plate instead of the obligation.

nodes.label: Garlicky Greens in Ten Minutes
nodes.blurb: Kale, chard, spinach — the technique is identical and it takes one pan and ten minutes. This is the side dish that goes with everything in this app.

nodes.label: Crispy Roasted Chickpeas
nodes.blurb: The snack that replaces the chip bag. Six grams of fiber a serving and they cost about fifty cents.

nodes.label: Almond-Date Energy Bites
nodes.blurb: No bake, no added sugar, five minutes in a food processor. The after-school food that is not a granola bar wrapper.

nodes.label: The Everyday Big Salad
nodes.blurb: Enough of a salad to be dinner. The rule is five textures, and once you see it you cannot unsee it.

nodes.label: Miso Butter Mushrooms on Toast
nodes.blurb: Mushrooms cooked past the point where they give up their water and start to brown, in butter cut with white miso. On thick toast this is lunch; on a small plate it is the thing people ask you to make again.

nodes.label: Crispy Smashed Potatoes with Garlic Aioli
nodes.blurb: Boiled until soft, squashed flat, then roasted hard so every ragged edge turns to glass. There is no better potato, and the five-minute lemon-garlic aioli is why the pan comes back empty.

nodes.label: Lemon Dutch Baby
nodes.blurb: Batter poured into a screaming hot buttered skillet, and twenty minutes later a pancake the size of the pan climbs up the sides and comes out looking like something that should not be possible at home.

nodes.label: Harvest Stuffed Acorn Squash
nodes.blurb: A centerpiece that doesn't apologise for not being a turkey. Roasted squash halves filled with wild rice, mushrooms, apples and pecans, glossed with cider.

nodes.label: Skillet Green Beans with Toasted Almonds
nodes.blurb: The green bean dish that replaces the casserole. Ten minutes, one pan, no canned soup, and it tastes like green beans on purpose.

nodes.label: Proper Herb Stuffing
nodes.blurb: Crisp on top, custardy underneath, and built on real bread and real herbs. It is a side dish, not an afterthought.

nodes.label: Real Cranberry Sauce with Orange
nodes.blurb: Twelve minutes, four ingredients, and half the sugar of the canned version. The one dish where homemade is not just better, it is faster.

nodes.label: Whipped Sweet Potatoes with Brown Butter and Sage
nodes.blurb: No marshmallows, no casserole. Just sweet potatoes tasting like themselves, with nutty brown butter and crisp sage on top.

nodes.label: Mushroom and Lentil Wellington
nodes.blurb: The showstopper. A deeply savoury mushroom-lentil filling wrapped in pastry, sliced at the table to an actual audible reaction.

nodes.label: Winter Citrus and Fennel Salad
nodes.blurb: Bright, cold and crunchy against a table of rich food. Ten minutes, and it is the plate everyone goes back to.

nodes.label: Hoppin' John
nodes.blurb: Black-eyed peas, rice and smoke — the New Year's Day pot that is supposed to bring luck, and definitely brings a cheap, excellent dinner.

nodes.label: Black Bean Burgers That Hold Together
nodes.blurb: The two failures of a bean burger are mush and blandness. Roasting the beans first fixes both. These grill without a cage and taste like something you'd order.

nodes.label: Grilled Vegetable Platter with Charred Scallion Sauce
nodes.blurb: The vegetable dish that stops being a side. Everything hits the grill, then gets piled on a platter under a bright green sauce.

nodes.label: Crunchy Picnic Slaw, No Mayo
nodes.blurb: Sits out on a table for three hours without anyone worrying. Sharper and crunchier than the creamy kind, and it gets better as it sits.

nodes.label: Grilled Corn with Chili, Lime and Cotija-Style Crumble
nodes.blurb: Ohio sweet corn, charred hard, rolled in lime and chili. Fifteen minutes and it is the first thing to disappear.

nodes.label: Watermelon, Feta and Mint
nodes.blurb: Three ingredients, no cooking, and the most refreshing thing on a hot table. Ten minutes with a knife.

nodes.label: Big-Batch Baked Ziti with White Beans
nodes.blurb: Feeds twelve, travels in the dish you baked it in, and reheats without complaint. The potluck workhorse.

nodes.label: Seven-Layer Bean Dip
nodes.blurb: The game-day dish that people stand around. Built on real refried beans and Greek yogurt instead of sour cream, and nobody can tell.

nodes.label: Buffalo Cauliflower Bites
nodes.blurb: Crisp, hot, and gone in ten minutes. Roasted rather than fried, so you can eat a plateful without regret.

nodes.label: Mediterranean Orzo Salad
nodes.blurb: Makes a bowl the size of a punchbowl, travels in a cooler, and is better an hour after you make it. The default potluck contribution.

nodes.label: Olive Oil Banana Bread
nodes.blurb: Moister than the butter version and it keeps better, which is exactly what a bake sale needs. One bowl, no mixer.

nodes.label: Chewy Oatmeal Cookies
nodes.blurb: Crisp edge, chewy middle, actual oat flavour. They travel well and they sell out first.

nodes.label: Dark Chocolate Olive Oil Brownies
nodes.blurb: Fudgy, glossy-topped, and made with olive oil instead of a stick of butter. Nobody guesses.

nodes.label: Overnight Baked French Toast
nodes.blurb: Assembled the night before, baked while people open presents. Feeds eight and makes the house smell like a holiday.

nodes.label: Fifteen-Minute Chickpea Skillet
nodes.blurb: Pantry to plate in the time it takes to set the table. No chopping board required if you buy the spinach pre-washed.

nodes.label: Ten-Minute Egg Fried Rice
nodes.blurb: The reason to cook extra rice. Leftover rice, frozen peas, eggs, and dinner is done before anyone asks what's for dinner.

nodes.label: White Bean Melt
nodes.blurb: Twelve minutes, mostly under the broiler. Crunchy, savoury, melty, and built entirely from things already in the cupboard.

nodes.label: Loaded Sweet Potato, Two Ways
nodes.blurb: Microwave a sweet potato, open a can, and it is dinner. The lowest-effort real meal in the collection.

nodes.label: Spring Pea and Asparagus Tart
nodes.blurb: Green, elegant, and mostly assembly. It looks like it took all morning and takes forty minutes.

nodes.label: Whipped Feta with Hot Honey and Pistachios
nodes.blurb: Feta and yogurt beaten until it turns into something closer to a cloud, then flooded with warm chile honey. It takes eight minutes and it is always the first bowl to empty.

nodes.label: Skillet Garlic Bread with a Parmesan Crust
nodes.blurb: Garlic butter worked into a split baguette, then the cut face pressed into parmesan and crisped in a skillet until it forms a lacy golden crust. It is not the garlic bread from the freezer aisle.

nodes.label: Salted Tahini Chocolate Chip Cookies
nodes.blurb: Tahini gives these the savoury, slightly bitter edge that makes a chocolate chip cookie interesting instead of just sweet. Flaky salt on top, and the middles stay soft for days.

nodes.label: Skillet Peach and Blueberry Crumble
nodes.blurb: August peaches cooked down in the same pan they are baked in, under a buttery oat topping that stays crunchy. It goes in the oven while you eat and comes out at exactly the right moment.
